# Meridian Mobility: A Growth Story

Meridian Mobility launched in 2018 as a ride-hailing service in a
handful of mid-sized cities. Its early growth was fast and, for the
first three years, disciplined: expansion followed demand, not the
other way around, and the company reached operating breakeven in
its core market by year three — a milestone few competitors in the
sector managed on a comparable timeline [@demo2020scaling].

By 2021, Meridian's leadership team faced a choice common to
fast-growing platform companies: keep deepening the core ride-hailing
business, or use its funding momentum to move into an adjacent,
capital-intensive market. Table 1.1 summarizes the position each
option started from.

```{=latex}
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3\linewidth}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.28\linewidth}

\toprule\noalign{}

\cellcolor{giTableFirstColShade}Market maturity & Established, profitable & Unproven, capital-intensive \\
\arrayrulecolor{giTableDivider}\hline

\caption{\label{tbl-position}Meridian's starting position in each business line, 2021.}
\end{longtable}
```

The pattern this book uses Meridian to illustrate — a stable core
business set aside in favor of a harder, unproven one — recurs often
enough in platform-company case studies to be treated as a distinct
failure mode, not a one-off [@christensen2019innovation].
